script: On a Sunday in March I sent the same file to forty people, and my aunt has not spoken to me since. Eleven days before that, she stood up at my grandmother's funeral and told all forty of them that I had not visited her once in six years. She did not say it to me. She said it about me, while I was sitting in the second row. I did not correct her. I let her finish. My grandmother's nurse was at that funeral, standing at the back. I watched her face the whole time my aunt talked. She had been building to it for months. Every phone call she found a way in. He is busy. We cannot all be like him. Three people in that room had seen me at that home. My cousin had walked past me in that corridor. Not one of them said a word. What she did not know is that every care home in this state keeps a visitor log, and the state makes them hold on to it for seven years. You sign in at the desk, in pen. Mine cost eleven dollars and took four days. Two hundred and twelve visits. Every Sunday, most Wednesdays, every Christmas. That is not the part I sent them. The log does not only have my name in it. It has everybody's. My aunt had signed in twice. In six years. Twice. I would have left it there. Then I looked at the second date. The eleventh of March. I knew that date. That was the week my grandmother's account was emptied. The home called me about it, and my aunt was the one who told me it was probably a card skimmer, and that I should not upset her by asking. The first visit was the fourteenth of January. Same year. The other withdrawal. She did not stand up at that funeral to talk about me. She stood up because she knew the log existed. She needed all forty of them to already have an opinion before anybody thought to read it. I let her have eleven days of it. Then I sent it. No message. Just the file. Forty people heard her stand up and say it. All forty of them have read it now.
